name: Curry leaf (Murraya koenigii)
short: No human adverse-event data on curry leaf alone. Mixtures: mild joint pain, no serious events (1 trial, with tribulus); minor events in a third (1 trial). Mice, alkaloid fraction: no/minimal toxicity.
text: Safety evidence for curry leaf as a supplement is limited and comes mainly from combination products and animal studies. In a 12-week randomized double-blind trial in 46 men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, a capsule combining curry leaf and Tribulus terrestris leaf extracts, taken by mouth, was compared with tamsulosin; mild joint pain was the most common adverse event in both groups and no serious events occurred. In a 4-week randomized placebo-controlled crossover trial in 32 people with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome, a powder combining Murraya koenigii (curry; the abstract does not name the plant part), pomegranate and turmeric, taken by mouth as a decoction, appeared safe, but one third of patients reported at least one minor adverse event that might be related to the study interventions. In a 45-day study in 45 women with type 2 diabetes, curry leaf extract capsules lowered fasting and random blood sugar and HbA1c; the abstract does not report adverse effects or whether participants were taking diabetes medicines. In an animal study of a mahanine-enriched alkaloid fraction of Murraya koenigii developed for cancer treatment (the abstract does not name the plant part), mice fed the fraction as a single high dose or daily for up to 180 days showed no significant clinical signs of toxicity, which the authors summarised as no or minimal toxicity for up to 180 days. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
